subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: mapping needs, resources and who can help [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Papa's week on one page

Darshan,

I have put everything in one place so we can stop guessing. Papa has physio on Tuesdays and Fridays, and a heart check-up every second month with blood tests beforehand. Evenings are fine: you finish by five and I am home by six. Weekends are fine too. Costs are covered for now from his pension and what we each put in. What we cannot fill is weekday mornings. He needs help getting up, washed and to his tablets, and neither of us can be there before ten because of our offices. So the problem is not everything. It is the hours from seven to ten. Can we talk on Sunday about who or what could cover them? 🙂

Your sister,
Ankita

qa.q: Which hours are the real gap in Papa's week?
qa.a: Weekday mornings, the hours from seven to ten.

qa.q: What does Ankita's phrase "so we can stop guessing" suggest about how Ankita feels?
qa.a: It suggests Ankita feels worried and wants clarity, using facts on one page to replace vague worry.

qa.q: What other approach could they use to fill the morning gap?
qa.a: They could arrange a paid helper for those hours or ask one of their offices about flexible timing, because the page shows the gap is narrow and specific.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the email?
qa.a: Darshan may feel relieved to see the problem set out clearly without blame, and perhaps a little anxious about changing work hours.

grounding: Ankita maps Papa's visits, daily needs, availability and costs and finds that weekday mornings are the gap.

passage:
Madhav, you asked how I stopped feeling like I was drowning with Papa's care. It started with a sheet of paper. I'm Sharmila, and I make spreadsheets for a living, so of course it did.
After his stroke last year, everything felt urgent all the time. So one night I wrote four columns. What Papa needs: physiotherapy on Tuesdays and Fridays, the heart doctor every month, help bathing each morning, someone to sit with him at lunch. Who could help: me, my brother in Nagpur, my sister-in-law two streets away. When each of us is free. And what it costs.
When I filled it in, the picture was suddenly obvious. Evenings were covered. Weekends were fine. The real gap was weekday mornings: bathing and breakfast, when I'm on the train and my sister-in-law does the school run.
One gap, not a hundred. That I could actually solve.

qa.q: On which days does Sharmila's father have physiotherapy?
How did Sharmila feel before and after making the sheet?
qa.a: Sharmila felt like drowning, with everything urgent, and then relieved and more in control once the sheet showed only one real gap.

qa.q: What else could Sharmila do now that the gap is clear?
qa.a: Sharmila could look into a trained morning helper or ask the brother to share the cost, focusing on weekday mornings only.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's sister-in-law see the sheet?
qa.a: The sister-in-law can see her evening help counts and that mornings clash with the school run, so she isn't blamed for what she can't cover.

grounding: It shows a daughter listing her father's medical visits, daily support needs, family availability and costs, and finding that weekday mornings are the real gap.

Dilnaz sits next to me in the design studio, so I watched her work this out over a few lunch breaks. I'm Kiran, by the way.
Her father had been unwell since spring, and she'd been leaving early, coming in late, looking frayed. One Monday she opened a big sheet of chart paper on the lunch table and started writing.
Left side: her father's needs. Kidney check-ups every fortnight, medicines three times a day, help getting to the bathroom at night, a walk each evening. Right side: people. Her, her younger sister in college, her mother's cousin in the same colony. And beside each, the times they were free and roughly what outside help would cost.
By Thursday she had coloured the gaps in red. Only one block stayed red: weekday mornings, eight to one.
She tapped it with her pen. "That's it. That's the real problem." She looked calmer than she had in weeks.

qa.q: How often does Dilnaz's father have kidney check-ups?
How did Dilnaz seem to feel when she tapped the red block?
qa.a: She seemed calmer and more focused, relieved that the overwhelming problem had shrunk to one clear gap.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz do with the chart?
qa.a: She could share it with her sister and her mother's cousin so everyone sees the gap, and then look for help just for weekday mornings.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's sister see the chart?
qa.a: Her sister, busy with college, can see exactly where help is needed and where she is already counted, which may make it easier to offer specific time.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, a daughter mapping her father's needs, family availability and costs and discovering that weekday mornings are the real gap.
